ai.definition: Regolith sintering is a process that uses high-power lasers to heat and fuse the fine, granular material found on the lunar surface (regolith) into solid structures. This method can be used for constructing habitats or other infrastructure on the Moon.
ai.howItWorks: High-powered lasers are directed at layers of regolith, which is heated to a temperature where its particles melt and then re-solidify, forming a glass-ceramic matrix that binds the particles together into a solid structure. This process can be repeated in layers to build up walls or other structures.
ai.problemSolved: It addresses the challenge of constructing durable infrastructure on the Moon using local materials without the need for transporting heavy construction materials from Earth.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves selecting and preparing regolith samples, setting up laser equipment, and applying the sintering technique in a controlled environment. Initial tests are conducted in laboratories before scaling up to space applications.
ai.buildProcess: A layer of regolith is spread out on a platform, then heated by a laser to its melting point. The material cools and solidifies into a fused layer. This process is repeated until the desired structure is built.
ai.costDrivers: The cost drivers include the initial setup of equipment, the availability and quality of regolith samples, and the energy requirements for the sintering process.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: promising but requires further testing and development before practical application on a large scale.
ai.regulation: Currently, no specific regulations govern this technology. However, any space-based construction would need to comply with international space laws and agreements.
ai.risks: Technical risks include ensuring the structural integrity of the sintered materials in various lunar environments, potential contamination from off-gassing during the process, and the difficulty in achieving consistent results across different regolith samples.
ai.profitability: The technology is not yet profitable due to its experimental nature and the limited scope of current applications. Potential future profitability depends on widespread adoption for space construction projects.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on optimizing the sintering process, improving material properties, and scaling up production methods for practical use in space construction.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking.

glossary.def: The layer of loose, broken rock and dust covering solid rock on the surface of the Moon.
A process where particles are heated to a temperature below their melting point so that they adhere together without actually fusing into a single piece.

subsystems.name: Power and heat source
subsystems.role: delivers the concentrated energy that fuses soil grains together.
parts: photovoltaic array or fission surface power

subsystems.name: Beam delivery and optics
subsystems.role: shapes and aims the beam at the right spot with the right intensity.
parts: dust shielding and purge for lenses

subsystems.name: Regolith handling
subsystems.role: excavates, grades and spreads soil in thin, even layers.
parts: sieve or crusher to remove large rocks

subsystems.name: Positioning and motion
subsystems.role: moves the beam or the workpiece so that each pass overlaps the last.

subsystems.name: Process monitoring
subsystems.role: watches melt pool temperature so the soil is fused, not boiled or left loose.

subsystems.name: Sintered product
subsystems.role: the glass-ceramic solid that results — walls, pads, roads or shielding.
parts: anchor or foundation into compacted soil

buildSteps.title: Choose and prepare the site
buildSteps.detail: Flatten an area, remove large rocks and compact the top few centimetres so later layers sit on a stable base.

buildSteps.title: Mine and grade soil
buildSteps.detail: Excavate loose regolith, screen out cobbles, and dry or preheat it to drive off adsorbed gases that would otherwise bubble the melt.

buildSteps.title: Lay the first powder layer
buildSteps.detail: Spread regolith to a controlled depth of a few millimetres, roughly uniform across the build area.

buildSteps.title: Sinter the layer
buildSteps.detail: Scan the beam across the surface at a speed and power that raises the soil above roughly 1,000 °C, hot enough to fuse particles into a glass-ceramic without fully melting the bed. Overlapping passes knit the tracks together.

buildSteps.title: Cool under control
buildSteps.detail: In vacuum there is no air to carry heat away, so cooling is radiative and slow; the scan pattern and beam power are managed to keep thermal gradients from cracking the solid.

buildSteps.title: Stack the next layer
buildSteps.detail: A fresh layer of soil is spread over the fused one and the process repeats, building walls, berms or a landing pad upward and outward.

buildSteps.title: Finish and anchor
buildSteps.detail: Unfused powder is brushed away, edges are dressed, and the structure is tied into the ground or covered with loose soil for radiation shielding.

buildSteps.title: Inspect and commission
buildSteps.detail: Check for cracks, delamination and porosity; verify load-bearing, and if the structure is to hold pressure, line it with a separate sealed membrane.

prerequisites.tech: Lunar soil simulants for ground testing
prerequisites.why: you cannot iterate on a process you cannot test on Earth, and real samples are scarce.

prerequisites.tech: High-power lasers, optics and solar concentrators
prerequisites.why: the hardware exists industrially, but must be ruggedised for vacuum, dust and wide temperature swings.
sintering draws kilowatts for long periods, and a lunar night or shadow requires stored energy or fission power.
no operator is on site, so excavation, layering and beam control must run themselves.

prerequisites.tech: Heavy lunar landing and surface logistics
prerequisites.why: the equipment must first be delivered intact to the site.

pathway.milestone: laboratory sintering of simulant with lasers, microwaves and concentrated sunlight
pathway.unlocks: understanding of melt behaviour, porosity and cracking in vacuum.

pathway.milestone: a small robotic payload sinters a patch of real regolith on the Moon
pathway.unlocks: proof that the process survives dust, vacuum, low gravity and real soil.

pathway.milestone: automated build of dust-suppressing landing pads and roads near a landing site
pathway.unlocks: safer, more frequent landings and a hardened traffic route between assets.

pathway.milestone: sintered structural shells and radiation berms erected over habitat modules
pathway.unlocks: base mass shifted from Earth imports to local soil.

pathway.milestone: field-fabricated sintered structures at a permanent outpost
pathway.unlocks: expansion of a base without shipping every wall from Earth.
